Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Customs and Excise) moved the third reading of Bill No. 113, respecting the Department of National Revenue.

Mr. Speaker, it was my misfortune not to have been in my place in this chamber on Tuesday last when this bill was discussed. Had I been here I would have expressed my most cordial commendation of the character of the bill and of the proposal to create subdivisions in this department. I believe that the appointment of three commissioners will have the effect of expediting the business of the department, and of relieving the minister of an immense amount of routine which should not be saddled upon him. I would also have suggested-I observe there was a little discussion on the point-that the name " Department of National Revenue " should be altered. It was suggested when the bill was discussed that the title " Department of Dominion Revenue " should be substituted but that I think would not be appropriate. It will be within the recollection of hon. members that a few years ago it was thought advisable to change the name of the Department of Militia and Defence and it is now known as the Department of National Defence. To that alteration there could be no possible objection. The introduction of the aeroplane and the creation
of an air force have made necessary an enlargement of the description of the department, and " national defence " now correctly describes its function. In that case the question of provincial administration did not arise at all, because the matter of defence is one wholly within the jurisdiction of this parliament. But when you come to deal with revenue it seems to me that without straining the point, without chasing a shadow but with some degree of substance, it can be said that the revenues of the province of Quebec are Dominion or national revenues. The suggestion therefore that I would make to the Minister of Customs and Excise is that instead of using the words " national revenue " he should use the words " federal revenue". By doing so a clear distinction is made between provincial revenues and what we call Dominion revenues. There is a treasurer in each of the various provinces. It is quite conceivable that at any time in the future the provincial treasurer might be called the Minister of Provincial Revenue. Is it not logical and will it not better answer the purpose of the reorganization of the Department of Customs and Excise if the corollarial terms be Minister of Federal Revenue in respect of the revenue of the Dominion and Minister of Provincial Revenue in respect of the revenue of the province? That is the suggestion which I throw out now and which I would have thrown out before if I had had the good fortune to be present when the bill was before the House on a previous occasion. It is a simple matter, a matter of a few minutes, to make the change and I think it would be more appropriate.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
It might facilitate matters if I made a brief general statement to the committee. As is well known, an effort was made three years ago to place Canadian National branch -line construction upon a three-year

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
basis in order that the management of the National railways might be able to enter more intelligently upon their construction work from year to year and not be held up depending upon the progress of an individual session of /parliament. The last three-year program voted by the House has now been practically completed. Nineteen branch lines have been constructed, involving a mileage of 572 at an estimated cost of $14,964,000 under the last program completed this year. Two projects only were not proceeded with, one being Kingsclear-Vanceboro line which was rendered unnecessary by reason of running rights being secured over the Canadian Pacific, and the other being the Rosedale-Bullpound Creek line in connection with which I expect shortly to bring down a bill for an extension of time. With the exception therefore of one project the whole of the previous program has been or will be completed prior to the 31st August, 4927, when the three-year authority expires.
The program now presented by the management through me for the next three years is very comprehensive in character and it has been given wide publicity. It is recommended by the president and the board of directors to the consideration of the House. When this resolution passes, I hope to introduce fifteen separate bills based upon it, and later I hope to refer these fifteen bills to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, in order that the details of the proposal may be examined by the committee and a report made thereon to the House.

speechtext: I was out while the minister was making his statement. Do I understand him to say that the proposed Kingsclear-Vanceboro branch has been definitely abandoned?

The situation in respect to the requirements of this region has been under consideration for some time, and while we are not yet prepared to make any further recommendation than the construction of the two branches included in the above list, it is altogether likely that we will find it necessary to make a further recommendation after our studies are completed.

Section 2 agreed to.
On paragraph 3.

speechtext:

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Each of the branch lines proposed connects with the existing Canadian National System. I shall be glad to give details of the one under discussion if my hon. friend wishes. I am prepared to give details to this committee, or to the railway committee, just as this committee desires.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I think some details should be given now so that they will appear on Hansard, because we are all interested in this branch line development, and others, like myself, are not members of the special committee. Perhaps the minister would give us
C.N.H.-Branch Lines

just a short synopsis of the recommendations made by the management, especially with regard to the lines in Quebec. I know there has been a scheme on foot in the lake St. John district for the construction of a circular line around lake St. John. subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: The two branches which are dealt with in section 1 (a) and 1 (b), and in section 2 are both in the lake St. John area, one proceeding up the west shore of the lake, and the other going partly around the north shore.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The construction of this
circular line is not contemplated at present?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Not completely around the lake. I read the president's note on that in order to make clear that the railway company is of opinion that they may require to come back within the three year period with respect to certain proposals in various parts of Canada, and particularly with respect to the lake St. John area.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: If I am not out of order, I would like to ask the Minister of Railways if the government is giving any consideration to taking over the Kent Northern railway, the last branch line in the province of New Brunswick which has not been acquired by the Canadian National system. Is it the intention to take it over immediately, or is it intended not to take it over? How does the matter stand?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon.
riend's information is surely not correct when ne says that is the last branch in New Brunswick not taken over by the Canadian National.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I think it is.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: To commence with, my hon. friend would not describe the St. John Valley railway-

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I had forgotten that, but you are operating that road anyway.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I would prefer, of course, not to discuss at this stage a matter which is dealt with specifically in the Duncan report as a part of the maritime provinces' general problem. My hon. friend's question opens up a very wide field indeed in that connection.
I think the committee will see the force of that.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I notice that section 3
speaks of a cost of $69,700 per mile, and in Saskatchewan there is a branch line to be 
constructed at a cost of $25,000 per mile. Is this big difference largely due to the cost of the right of way?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not
that detailed information under my hand, but I will see that it is supplied in the railway committee. There will, of course, be a detailed estimate before that committee in the hands of the officers of the company.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Are these branch lines
simply to gather the local traffic, or are they a part of the main line system?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Is the department really undertaking to build more colonization roads?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Both the Canadian
National and the Canadian Pacific are reaching out into the newer parts of Canada very rapidly. Both railways have found it profitable to do so, the Canadian Pacific especially. One of the criticisms of this parliament which is being heard more and more frequently is that the Canadian Pacific is reaching out into new country at a faster rate than the Canadian National, and the object of this branch line program is to give the Canadian National the opportunity of reaching out into the newer developed sections of Canada, in order to build feeders for the Canadian National sytem.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I do not think the hon. minister caught my point. Is it the policy to build purely colonization roads irrespective of the traffic available at the present time?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
It is very difficult to
know exactly what my hon. friend means by that term-"purely colonization roads." If he means lines which as they are built tend to open up the country and bring in settlers, and thus produce traffic progressively year by year, yes, that is the policy of the Canadian National, and it is supported by the Department of Railways and Canals.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
But are you building
these ahead of settlement?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I would not say that we would adopt the policy of going in ahead of settlement, but, fortunately or unfortunately, there are many areas of Canada into which

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
settlement has gone fifty and sixty and in some cases up to one hundred miles ahead of the railway, in varying degrees, and it is into that type of settlement that the railways, both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National are being pushed. Always when a line is built into such a district the settlement increases very rapidly, and consequently the traffic increases rapidly also.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I understand that this is
a program covering three years. There is no doubt at all in my mind that such a policy is necessary due to the growth of the country, for to operate properly the system must have feeders. But I would like to ask the minister whether we are to understand that no branch line construction outside of this program now brought down will be considered during the next three years which it is supposed to cover.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I should again in that
connection quote from the president's memorandum, which I read a short time ago. After dealing with the lake St. John district, as to which the president specifically stated that further studies were being undertaken in that neighbourhood which might make it necessary for the company to come back again to parliament, he says also:
Of course it may also be found desirable to ask later on for one or two other extensions, as a result of development not fully foreseen at this time.
That is to say while we are providing for a three year policy of construction, our hands are not completely tied and we are not prevented from considering projects which may develop as a result of things which are not foreseen at the moment.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
That satisfies me in
regard to something unforeseen at the moment, but I am referring to some branch lines in the maritime provinces which have been discussed in this House several times, and as a matter of fact I think have been authorized by this House on two occasions. The program, as the minister has outlined it, calls for an expenditure in the prairie provinces of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000 and over $5,000,000 in the province of Quebec. I should like to know if, in regard to branch lines, the door is closed to Nova Scotia for three years.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: The door of the president of the Canadian National Railways is never closed with respect to branch lines. My hon. friend will have in future the same opportunity as he and all others have had in the past of attempting to convince the management of the Canadian National Railways that any given proposal should be recommended by them to the government.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Many of us are not members of the railway committee, and here is an outstanding item which I think must have caught the minister's eye and in regard to which I should like some explanation. Section 2 speaks of seven miles of railway from a point near Grand Mere on the Canadian Northern Quebec railway, at an estimated cost of $213,038 per mile. Can we not get some explanation?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I am sorry I did not
bring my estimates with me. I did not consider all the estimates would be required in committee, but I have here some indication of the motive for the line in question. I have a summary of the information later to be laid before the railway committee.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Most of us are not members of that committee and we would like an explanation of an outstanding figure such as this.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
This branch would leave the present line at Grand Mere and keeping in the valley of the St. Maurice river swing south of the present line into the town of Shawinigan Falls, then head generally northwest and rejoin the present main line at East Burrills about two and a half miles west of Glenada station. The present line from Grand Mere to East Burrills and the spur Aldred to Shawinigan Falls would be (abandoned. This branch line will accomplish two tilings. It will reduce the present steep gradient westbound out of Grand Mere, which is now 1.5 per cent to 0.6 per cent and give direct main line connection to the town of Shawinigan Falls.
The big economy however, comes from the reduction of gradients on the main line. At Garneau Junction, three miles west of Grand Mere come together the line from Quebec and the line from the north, which brings business from the lake St. John district, as well as from the National Transcontinental railway. The westbound tonnage from Garneau Junction to Montreal is concentrated and therefore heavier than east of Garneau Junction. At present the westbound gradient immediately out of Grand Mere controls the trainload into Montreal. By the proposed gradient improvement at this one place on the main line, the westbound freight train tonnage can be increased immediately by 79 per cent and eventually when a few other changes have been made in the line west into Joliette, the tonnage of trains westbound can
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

be better than doubled. This means that on completion of this line 45 per cent of the freight train miles can be saved on business moved, and, with the further grade revision into Joliette complete, the freight train miles can be more than cut in two for a given business.
This will give my hon. friend an indication of the reasons why it is necessary to spend a large sum of money. Without having the details before me, I may say in a general way that on the Canadian National system there are many places where, when the line was first constructed, a roundabout route and a heavy gradient were adopted in order to avoid the greater expense which would be involved in going more directly and on a lower grade. This is one outstanding case. It is very obvious that when the line was first built the cheapest possible route was adopted, producing heavy grade conditions. We are able, by spending a lot of money, as my hon. friend points out, to reduce the grade and double the trainload westbound into Montreal, and it will therefore pay for itself in a short time.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I concede that that might justify the construction of the railway, but it does not give me any information as to why a mile there should cost $213,000, and other sections cost only $50,000 and $25,000 a mile respectively. Why should the railway cost this large sum of money?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
A question has been asked
as to why this line should cost as much as $213,038 per mile, and I think we should have an answer.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to
say on at least three occasions, in reply to that question this afternoon, that I have not with me complete particulars of the engineer's estimated cost of every mile proposed to be built, because in the past I have found that such details have been gone into in the select committee, and I did not come prepared with that information. I would require to have a great volume of information on my desk in order to answer that question, and I have not the information at present. Any members of this House who are not members of the railway committee can attend the sittings of that committee, if it is convenient for them to do so, and I will be very glad indeed to have a complete memorandum for the information of my hon. friend in that committee. I cannot pretend to carry all the details in my head. I have not on my desk at the present time the large volume of information which necessarily accompanies these branch line proposals.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The line starts at Grand
Mere and runs to what point?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Back to the main line
again.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
But where to? If it ran
through Montreal we could easily understand the reason of the heavy cost.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
It is only seven miles
long.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Where does it begin and
where does it end?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: It runs from Grand Mere to Shawinigan Falls and back to the main line at East Burrills. Maps have been supplied for members of the committee indicating in a general way the details of each one of the proposals. I think my hon. friend has the map.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: That is all right, but paragraph 2 is a little short in its information and is not property drafted.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right
about that but it is in proper shape in the bill itself.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend indicated
that this program comprised all the work to be done within the next three years. I hope my hon. friend will be able to assure the House that during the next three years he will not permit any order in council to go through for the construction of a branch like the Rouyn railway. This was not included in the program of the last three years. It never came before the House but was put through quietly by order in council at a cost of $5,000,000. I hope this will not occur again.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The minister is not
quite frank with us. He comes to the House with a large order and is not prepared to give us any information at all. He practically asks us to delegate our functions and our ability to the railway committee, on which three-quarters of the members do not sit. There are many committee meetings to be attended, and these bills ought not to go through the House without adequate information. We are going to vote millions of dollars regarding the expenditure of which we shall be altogether ignorant. I repeat, the minister is not very frank with us.

Section agreed to.
On section 4.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The mileage provided for Alberta is approximately sixty-eight, and the

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
total expenditure on the different branch lines in Alberta is $2,479,000. The branch lines of Saskatchewan approximate 293 miles and involve an expenditure of $9,629,000. I want to commend the minister for making provision to meet the needs of the farmers of these two provinces, while at the same time bringing additional traffic to the national system. But I trust, in view of these figures and the large expenditure made in the province of Saskatchewan, he will keep the needs of Alberta in mind when he is urged later to provide additional mileage to serve the Peace River district, and to provide an outlet to the coast for the people there.

Section agreed to.
On section 5.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: What is the objective of this particular branch? Are the railway officials aiming at any particular point in the extension of the Willow Brook branch?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The Willow Brook situation has developed as the result of a tentative arrangement between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National to serve an area which lies between the Canadian Pacific Winnipeg-Edmonton main line and the former Grand Trunk Pacific main line of the Canadian National. There is rather a wide gap through there. The Canadian Pacific gave notice of their intention to ask parliament for a charter covering the territory in question, but it appeared that as a consequence of granting that charter the Canadian Pacific would parallel the main line of the Canadian National for a distance of between forty and fifty miles at not much more than ten miles. Naturally the Canadian National objected, but they indicated their willingness to extend the Willow Brook branch into that area and to serve part of it at the present time, and later on as much of it as might be necessary. Both railways came to me as minister and I suggested that if they were still in disagreement, the railway committee would deal with the matter and decide which line should serve the territory in question. I suggested, however, that they might possibly facilitate matters for parliament by discussing the subject and agreeing to some method of serving the territory without duplication. After they had reached an agreement with the Canadian National on the division of the territory, the Canadian Pacific's proposals were considered by the railway committee, and a few days ago a bill came before the House. This short line represents the extension of the
Canadian National railway to serve that part of the area which it was agreed they, should serve. This territory will be fairly well served as a result of the arrangement made. Possibly in the future some further mileage may be required in addition to the line now proposed, but we can best decide that after the details have been worked out as a result of construction.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: It is important to avoid duplication which, whether the road be built by a private company or by the government, must hurt us nationally. In this instance I should prefer to have seen all that particular territory served by the Canadian National because it is a rich district and the revenue would be considerable. However, it is much more desirable to have an arrangement between the two companies so that there may be no duplication, rather than have the two lines closely paralleling each other, as they would have done had the whole territory been intersected by both.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
What is the average
distance between the present main line of the Canadian Pacific and the main line of the Canadian National?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: It is hard to average the distance over the area inasmuch as it varies considerably, as hon. members of the railway committee will remember after having seen it illustrated on the map. Speaking offhand, however, I should think that the maximum distance between the two roads in a direct line would be about forty miles, which probably would narrow down in some places to about thirty-five miles. My hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) is fairly familiar with the territory and will confirm that statement.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
There are two areas there
which need railway service, one north and one south of the Canadian National main line. One would have thought that the natural thing to do would be for the Canadian Pacific to take one territory and the Canadian National the other, but instead of that a ridiculous arrangement is made between the two companies. Both go into the same territory and encroach on each other, and the people are not served as well as they would be if one railway went right through. It seems to me that this is a problem which will become graver as time goes on, and I do think that throughout Canada, but particularly in the west, some arrangement should be arrived at whereby a committee of experts might lay out the territory for all new railways to be built from now on, indicating where lines are needed and wherein the service can be given most
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

economically. Anyone taking a casual view of the matter must conclude that it is a childish thing for the two railways to be quarrelling over some small bit of territory when so much railway accommodation is called for in other parts of the country. I cannot see why the Canadian National should not have taken the territory north of the main line and the Canadian Pacific the part south. As I say, the people would have been better served and it would have been more economical.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: There is a real difficulty in this district, as my hon. friend (Mr. Evans) has indicated. As one looks at the lines on the railway map it certainly seems ridiculous to allow the Canadian Pacific to get in a little loop there which appears to be directly in the route of the Canadian National branch line from Willowbrook, but I presume under the circumstances that the department must consider the interests of both railways and divide the territory 'between them accordingly. This again brings to mind the difficulties with which we are confronted and with which we will always be confronted until a solution is found. I know that the suggestion that the Canadian Pacific railway be nationalized will be laughed at in this House and almost everywhere throughout the country to-day, but to my mind it is the only practical solution of these troubles. At some time in the future, it may be twenty-five years from now, this House will have to face that situation.

Section agreed to.
On section 6:

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: In regard to this paragraph it would seem that the objective of this branch is the Hudson Bay railway, because it touches the Prince Albert branch at a point I would judge to be twenty-five or thirty miles west of Hudson Bay Junction. Is that on account of engineering difficulties, or is it not the objective of this branch to connect that country with the Hudson Bay railway and if so why does it not connect at the junction itself?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
This branch will run
from a point near Sturgis to a point between Crooked River and Mistatim, and is desired by the management of the railway apart altogether from the partial link it would provide with the Hudson Bay railway; it is desired for operating purposes largely. In fact it will have a three-fold purpose; it will be part of a line from Sturgis to Hudson Bay Junction, as indicated by my hon. friend, and will thereby open up a large area of good agricul-

tural land; then it will provide railway transportation to the soldier settlement south of Prairie River. The main feature, however, is to provide a shorter and better through route for the business of the Melfort and Prince Albert districts to Winnipeg and the head of the lakes. It is estimated that the saving on through traffic by this route would amount to $48,000 per year in operation.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
There is another difficulty which I might mention in connection with this branch. Hon. members will recall that in 1924 a bill passed this House providing for a branch from Kelvington to a point about Tisdale, on the Prince Albert branch. When the bill was thrown out by the Senate the Canadian Pacific Railway immediately started work on a branch from Sheho, running from ten to twenty miles west of the proposed branch of the Canadian National Railways. A lot of the country through which the Canadian Pacific railway line runs is a rather swampy and bushy district, and the villages contained therein are very difficult of access. To the east of that line, along the proposed route of the Canadian National branch line, there is an excellent farming country; I think it no exaggeration to say that there is no finer or more productive piece of agricultural country in western Canada than will be found in the district between Kelvington and Tisdale, and it is nothing short of a tragedy that this particular branch line was turned down at that time. Of course I hold the government partly responsible for this, because I think they should have gone on with that work by providing the necessary amount in the estimates. A great many people went into that district when the line was surveyed expecting the branch to be constructed in due time, and even after the resolution appeared on the order paper here a great many people moved in and took up residence in that particular district. The rejection of the proposed line has left these people in a very unfortunate position; hundreds of them have moved off the land while others are remaining and trying to farm under great difficulties, hauling their grain very long distances to the railway. May I refer particularly to the district around Perigord, and I think the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) will endorse what I have to say, because he is familiar with that district. It is one of the finest districts that can be found in western Canada, and is an exceptionally rich agricultural country. People went in there, broke up large areas of land and built good houses

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
anticipating that a branch line would be built, but to-day they are obliged to haul their grain from twenty to twenty-five miles. These people are left in a position where they hardly know whether to carry on or whether to move out. They are still hoping that at some time in the future this original branch line will be constructed, and are holding on in that hope.
I may say that the branch line now under consideration will take in the northern part of that territory which would have been served by the original branch line, and will perhaps limit the chances of these people to get another branch line at some future time. Of course I am speaking without knowledge of the engineering difficulties and other conditions, but ordinarily if this branch had been built to connect directly with Hudson Bay Junction it would have served what I believe was one of its original purposes. That is, it would have opened up all that country south of the Hudson Bay railway and would have left a sufficiently large area to be provided w'ith a further branch line at some future time. I do hope that when this line is built it will strike the main line at a point further east, if there are no engineering or other difficulties in the way.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I should say a word or
two in connection with the matter my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) has just referred to. This branch is in his own constituency, and he knows it very well. He also knows, of course, that for a number of years before I bad the honour of occupying my present office it was my duty in a former capacity to make representations to the railway authorities with regard to the area which he mentions, more particularly the Perigord and Farmingdale districts. I am now in the position of putting before this House what the management of the Canadian National Railways recommends, after duly considering the very many branch line proposals from one end of Canada to the other. With regard to the line now under discussion, which does not serve the Perigord and Farmingdale districts, I might Say that the management of the Canadian National Railways have been endeavouring for many years to secure a route across from the Melfort-Prince Albert line to the Swan river line, which would offer operating advantages superior to the route around the big loop by Hudson Bay junction. This line has been chosen largely because it offers these operating advantages which could not be obtained by a line running straight north from Kelvington. I would also point out that the soldier settlements south of Prairie River and Mistatim are at present
in quite as difficult a situation as the Perigord and Farmingdale districts, and it was impossible to so plan this line as to serve at one and the same time those soldier settlements and the Perigord area; that proved to be impossible. I can only say with regard to the Perigord proposal that the management does not recommend it at present. I have here some notes respecting applications which have been made during the last two years; I am afraid it will take too long to place on Hansard the detailed information involved, but I will be very glad to communicate to my hon. friend, who is of course the only member directly interested, the report of the president with respect to the whole matter, which takes up some four pages of my notes. Perhaps my hon. friend would be satisfied with that.
Section agreed to.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
May I ask with regard
to paragraph 7 just how the railway contemplated there will run with respect to the C.P.R. branch line? I think there is a branch connecting with the next town of Tisdale. Would not the branch proposed here closely parallel the Canadian Pacific railway?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend is in
error when he says that Tisdale is the next station. He is not apparently as familiar with the area in question as I thought he was.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I might say that I was
studying the Canadian National railway folder, but I realize there are flag stations in between that are not mentioned there. It is only the largest stations apparently that are mentioned on this map.

speechtext:

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Another point to which I
should like to draw the attention of the minister is this:	Can the treasury stand a program of such enormous expenditures? I wish to point out to the minister in all seriousness that this money which is being expended is being expended largely in one portion of Canada-you have nothing there for the expansion and development of eastern Canada. Surely you can devote a few hundred thousand dollars of the money which is being expended in colonization to expenditure in eastern Canada. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are being spent in the west for hotels that are losing enormous sums yearly. 'The minister may shake his head but I affirm that they are. Their operation is improving a little, and I

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
am very glad of it, but in 1924 the Fort Garry hotel in Winnipeg lost $193,000 without allowing for depreciation or interest on the money. Other items of the same kind may be cited. I wish to remind the minister that people in eastern Canada expect some development and wish to see a portion of the money which is being expended in other directions spent in their neighbourhood.
We hear a great deal about summer resorts. The Canadian National spend enormous amounts of money on Jasper lodge and in other portions of western Canada. In my constituency in tlhe town of Shediac there is one of the finest summer resorts in Canada to-day where everything can be had in the way of sea food, oysters, lobsters, and all kinds of fish during the proper season. There is an opportunity to build a hotel there. If money must be spent on hotels, let us have some of these expenditures in eastern Canada. Let us have an opportunity to develop along with the rest of Canada. Let us feel the pulse beat of development as it is felt in other parts of the country, and let our Canadian National railways be a credit to the people of the whole of Canada and have a tendency more than they have had in the past to develop our country and to make us all feel that we are going along, working together, to make an united Dominion.
This railway proposition is a mighty one; it is a hard thing to handle; but I believe it can be used as an agency for greater development in Canada than we have had in the past and for bringing about a much better feeling among the people, the east and the west. I would earnestly urge the minister to see to it that his department of colonization endeavours to make a more thorough investigation into maritime problems and to see if some way cannot be devised to remedy conditions as they exist there to-day. The maritime provinces are anxiously waiting for action on the Duncan report,'and the government of to-day is on trial as to what is going to be done to remedy the disabilities of the mari-times. I trust the Minister of Railways as well as the other ministers of the government are giving serious consideration to the situation as it exists because the people of the maritimes are much in earnest at the present time. They feel that they have borne the burden more heavily than any other portion of Canada. They feel that they have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in the development of other portions of the country with very little or no return. I would ask the minister and the other ministers of the government to consider the situation seriously and see if something cannot be done to 32649-68
improve conditions in the maritime provinces.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I do not want to drift
into a discussion on maritime rights and I will not follow my hon. friend along that line. In so far as his remarks relate to this program, may I point out that it is recommended by the management and board of directors of the Canadian National as being in the best interests of the success and prosperity of the National system of lines; that on the board of directors and management there is a considerable majority of eastern Canadians, and to create the impression, as my hon. friend's remarks undoubtedly would whether he so intended or not, that some special privilege was being extended to western Canada through this program is, I can assure him, entirely wrong. The board of directors is composed very largely of men from eastern Canada. There are only two from west of the great lakes. As everyone in this House knows, the management is certainly not western in any sense of the word.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: There is one from the maritime provinces, Mr. Lodge. I do not know of any other.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
and I do not understand each other. Evidently when my hon. friend was referring to eastern Canada he wias not using the term in the same sense that I am using it now. When I speak of eastern Canada I mean that broad division lying east of the great lakes. My hon. friend evidently meant the maritime provinces when he spoke of eastern Canada and therefore to that extent I misunderstood him.
While the criticism may be urged that this development program so far as it relates to branch lines is largely in western Canada, 1 would again point out to the committee that the great privately-owned corporation, who are certainly not playing favorites, who are looking after the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific at all times, are looking after this part of Canada which we are dealing with in this resolution. That proves that it is good business.
With respect to hotels, might I point out that last year during the hectic period which we had in this House, representations were made to me by the Hon. E. M. Macdonald, and I believe also by the present member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) with respect to a hotel in the maritime provinces, at Pictou, if my memory serves me aright? That matter was investigated by the Canadian National management ; they recommended its purchase, and to-day it is a Canadian National summer hotel.

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: On a very small scale.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I presume so. But, like Jasper Park, if it pays, you can depend upon the management extending it in proportion to the patronage it receives. The Canadian National railway management is on the job as regards improving facilities which bring in revenue to the National lines.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: I very much regret speaking in a sectional way in dealing with this railway branch line program now before the House, but I confess I was disappointed when this project was brought down. This was largely the reason of my question to the minister this afternoon when I asked if only branch lines suggested by the management were submitted to the House. I had reference particularly to the Guysborough railway. While the representative from that constituency is not in his seat I am sure that railway has the sympathy of the present management of the Canadian National system. I was glad that the minister this afternoon stated to the committee that the door was not closed for the next three years in relation to additional railway lines.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: And if it was, I can assure my hon. friend that the present member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) has told me that, if necessary, he intends to break the door open.	.

speechtext: I am glad to hear that. The minister made some reference to the new bungalow hotel system as it was introduced in that province. speechtext: Thank you. tioned by the hon. member was before the House, the Right Hon. Mr. Graham being then Minister of Railways, the only opposition to it came from the other side of the House; that with all that opposition the bill was passed in this House, and that it was thrown out by the Senate?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Before the resolution is reported I would like to make a few observations on the program and also to secure some information from the minister. It is quite true the Canadian National board may think it is sufficient for the present time, but there are other railway projects very much needed in western Canada, and which should, in my judgment, be included in this program. First, I should like to get some information from the minister with reference to what is known as the joint section from Rosedale to Bullpound Creek. This passed the House three years ago. It is a joint section to be built by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. I understand that there is some agreement between these two companies with regard to this joint section, and that the appropriation will run out some time in June, I think. I would ask the minister whether any provision is going to be made for the payment of the half share of the Canadian National in the construction of this joint section.

speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend

speechtext:
There are one or two
other branch lines to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister. I should be very glad to know if the minister has any information that he can give to the House as to the reason why this particular construction is not going to be proceeded with. During the last few years many of the people left the district traversed by this particular railway, but since the portion was completed and put in operation last year many of the old residents have come back, and the development that has taken place there in the last two years is enormous. So this particular line at least is assured of a much higher tonnage than could have been expected when the line was first extended from Lovema westward. Does the management intend to ask for power to build this line in the near future, or what recommendations has the minister from the management in regard to it?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
The line is not included in the program before the House, and it is not the intention to introduce legislation regarding it at this session, because it has not been recommended to the government by the management of the Canadian National Railways. I am afraid in that regard I cannot add anything to what the president informed my hon. friend under date of January 12. The people of this area and, indeed, in all the others-there are very many of them; I have here a whdle file of requests for branch lines in all parts of Canada which have not been included in the program now before the House-to the people of each district I would say that they have the opportunity of convincing the management of the Canadian National Railways that the line in question is a sound proposition from the 32649-68i
point of view of the Canadian National and should be recommended by them to the government. That is all I can say to my hon. friend, who I think is familiar with the position in that regard, and desires to have it as a matter of record.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: There is another railway in that district further south, known as the Eyre-Acadia valley line. This was built in connection with the joint section from Rose-dale to Bullpound. The grade was built in the year 1921, and only something like twenty miles of steel has been laid from Eyre to Acadia valley. There were from twenty to twenty-dive miles of grade built in 1921, on which no steel has been laid. The people leel that once the grade has been built, in view of the smaller cost of laying the steel upon the line, the steel should be laid at an early date, in order that the people in that district may have the transportation facilities they have been expecting for some years. A problem has loomed up, however, in the last year or two. It was contemplated in 1919, when the joint charter was given to the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, that the Canadian Pacific would proceed in an easterly direction from Bullpound towards Empress. I understand, however, that the Canadian Pacific have virtually given up the idea of building that particular line, and consequently the other question crops up, that in order to give the people close to the Red river the service that is very requisite, it might be desirable to re-survey the whole project from Acadia valley -to Bullpound. I do not know whether the minister has any notes or recommendations from the management in regard to that or not, but if he has, I would like to know what is contemplated.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, this matter is under investigation by the management at the present time, and there is involved in it also negotiations with the Canadian Pacific with respect to the Rosedale-Bullpound line. I should like to say for the information not only of my hon. friend, but of the committee in general that the assumption that the grading represents the major cost in building a line of railway is not correct. The steel and ties and labour, after the grading is done, are far, far more expensive than the cost of building the grade in the first place.

I particularly appreciate that because I know there are many men on this side of the House, as well as the other, who should to-day be placing something on Hansard for the benefit of their constituents, but who are refraining from so doing, knowing full well that they must deal with the management of the Canadian National Railways in the first instance.
I regret that I cannot say anything more with respect to other branch line proposals. If I had the information as to the intention of the management I would be glad to give it, but I do not have it before me in any of these particular cases, because these matters are still under consideration by the management.

speechtext: I suppose when the bill is before the committee some of the officials will be there to give us important information to clear up some of the matters upon which we have no information?

speechtext:

will recall, I think, that last year, when the railway estimates were under consideration by the committee, I called attention to a small line branching off the Canadian National railway at Maccan, in Nova Scotia, running to the town of Joggins on the bay of Fundy. speechtext: Is that Joggins?

speechtext:

road and its equipment are in a deplorable condition. The road serves a country very rich in coal, agriculture and timber. The minister last year promised some consideration with regard to the proposed absorption of this line by the Canadian National Railways. It is very difficult to bring the matter to the railway board other than through the medium of this House, as I understand it. And considering the fact that there is to be an expenditure of $20,000,000 for a program of railway construction covering three years, most of which is going to other parts of Canada, I think that this is one railway service in the east which should be given some attention by the Minister of Railways, and I would ask him if he has investigated this project, and with what result?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
I hope this is not a preliminary to what might easily happen; that is that members from other parts of Canada where there are some privately owned railways, or some lines of railway not now owned by the Canadian National, will endeavour to get us to take over their particular lines. One of the greatest difficulties in connection with the Canadian National! system at the present time is the number of lines here and there over Canada, which are not now owned by the Canadian National system, but by the provinces in some cases, and in the majority of cases by private corporations, which are desirous of selling their property to the Canadian National system.
I do not want to enter into a discussion, of the problems in the maritime provinces and eastern Quebec which are involved in considerations of that kind. I can only say that the Joggins line is a small, small part of a very great problem, and I can assure my hon. friend that the Joggins line will not be lost sight of when we are considering means of dealing effectively with the much larger problem involved. I see that my hon. friend from

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) is chafing at the bit just now. He wants to tell us what should he done with respect to the Gaspe railway, and I say that the railway situation at Joggins is nothing compared to what may be said with reference to Bonaventure, or what the hon. the Speaker might have to say with resipect to the situation in the Gaspe peninsula. These are not the only ones. This matter represents one of the problems we have not yet solved, I frankly admit it is difficult to deal with, and I do not think it will be helped by attempting to deal with one of the many smaller propositions. We must look at it as a general problem, as relating to a very large section of the maritime provinces particularly, and also eastern Quebec.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Has the minister considered the Lake St. John railway proposition?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: The Lake St. John proposition has already been before the committee.

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext: Is this the complete program for the next few years, or is it open to further extension? I desire also to ask, if this is the entire program recommended by the Canadian National Railways, or have some of the recommendations been turned down by the government?

subtopic: BRANCH LINES CONSTRUCTION-RESOLUTION
speechtext:
None of them has been
turned down. With reference to the three year program, we are endeavouring to so plan the addition to capital expenditure of the Canadian National as to keep well within bounds. Naturally in so doing it is advisable to endeavour to budget for a considerable period ahead1 and to hold down capital extensions to the system, except where they are demonstrated as being both necessary and good from the point of view of revenue. In saying that I do not mean to imply that we intend to come down each year with a new three-year policy of extension. As far as we can now foresee, this is our program for the next three years, but in connection with such a great system it would be absurd to take the ground that we will not at the next session of parliament introduce any branch line legislation, but broadly, this is our program for the next three years.
