subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS

speechtext:
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Judges Act, chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, to provide:-*
1.	That a salary of $12,000 per annum be granted for one additional judge of the Supreme Court of Canada;
2.	That on his attaining or having attained the age of seventy-five years, any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or of the Exchequer Court of Canada may be granted an annuity equal to that which he would then have been eligible to receive if this legislation had not been passed and if be had at that time resigned liis office.
3.	That if the said Judge be not then eligible for the grant of an annuity, and was appointed before the passing of this legislation, or if he was appointed after the passing of this legislation and has continued in office for at least ten years, he may be granted an annuity equal to two-thirds of his salary at the time he ceased to hold such office.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
This resolution precedes the introduction of three bills; one to amend the Supreme Court Act, another to amend the Exchequer Court Act and the third to amend the Judges Act. The first clause of the resolution provides for the granting of a salary for one additional judge of the Supreme Court of Canada. The two other -clauses of the resolution, which have been prepared by the officers of the House from copies of the bills which have been supplied -to them,
provide for the retirement of the judges of the Supreme Court or of the Exchequer Court of Canada when they have reached the age of seventy-five years. These are the financial arrangements to supply them with a pension to which they would otherwise be entitled.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: Is that voluntary retirement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
No, they would -cease
to hold office at the age of seventy-five years. These two changes are made for the same reasons.' The Supreme Court -of Canada is the highest tribunal of the land and it is of the utmost importance that it should have and retain -the confidence of the people and be maintained in the highest state of efficiency. When the Supreme -court was established and constituted the number -of judges was the same as it is to-day-six, one chief justice and five puisne judges. Since then the country has developed tremendously and the importance of -the cases to be decided is much greater. While geographical conditions should not be considered in the appointment of judges, because the best possible men should be appointed to the Supreme Court of Canada, there is -one exception, namely that two judges will always be members of the bench or -bar of Quebec, familiar with the civil law -and procedure of -that province. Apart from that there is no geographical condition mentioned in the act. I must say, however, that since the creation of the court such considerations have been -taken into account in making appointments; there is one judge usually supposed to be a member of the bar or bench of one of the maritime provinces; two -come from Quebec; two have usually been appointed from Ontario and one judge is usually appointed from the bench of British Columbia. The prairie provinces were not then developed as they are to-day, and up to the present there -has not been a judge from either the bar or the bench of any of those provinces. It has happened quite frequently -that when one or two judges are sick or unable to sit, or when some of them -are disqualified through having already given an opinion on the matter submitted to the court, -the chief justice has been compelled to ask a member of another court, either from Ontario or Quebec or some other province, to sit as a member -of that tribunal. It has been represented to me many times that that does not make for the full efficiency of the court, and that litigants who come from all parts of Canada and who spend a considerable amount of money to secure the decision of the highest court of the land are entitled to have their cases heard and decided by judges having the standing of the Supreme
Judges Act Amendment

Court of Canada. This is also the practice prevailing in other countries; the Supreme Court of Australia consists of seven judges, the exact number we will have in Canada if this bill becomes law.
There is another consideration which applies to the provision making retirement compulsory at seventy-five years of age. Members of the bar come to argue cases before the Supreme court from distant parts of the country, and the court must be complete and well organized in order to hear these oases when counsel come to Ottawa for that purpose. Such cases camnot be adjourned except at considerable expense and to the disadvantage of the litigants and the members of the bar as well. These considerations apply as well to the other clauses of the bill making the retirement of the judges of the Supreme court and the Exchequer court compulsory at the age of seventy-five years.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
Does that mean the Supreme
Court of Canada alone, or does it include the Supreme courts in the various provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I will come to that in
a moment. I notice that my good friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) has a resolution on the order paper asking that all judges should be retired when they reach the age of seventy-five years. I believe that under the British North America Act we have not the right to do that in the case of the judges of the high courts of Canada. The sections of the British North America Act dealing with the judicature are 96, 97, 98, 99, 100 and 101. Section 99 states, that the .judges of the superior courts shall hold office during good behaviour but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons. According to the enactment the tenure of the judges of the high courts of Canada is really a life tenure, and this parliament has no right to retire them compulsorily at any time during good behaviour.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: I grant that the contention is right in regard to existing judges, but what about appointments in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I am afraid that we
could not meet the wishes of my hon. friend unless we asked for an amendment to the British North America Act. We have the right so far as the Supreme court and the Exchequer court are concerned because of the provisions of section 101, which reads! as follows:
The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this act, from time to time, provide for the constitution, maintenance, and organization of a general court of appeal for

Canada, and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
The Supreme Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court of Canada have been created and constituted in virtue of section 101 of the British North America Act, which especially states that notwithstanding anything in the act, notwithstanding section 99 or any other section, pariiament had the right, when creating the Supreme court, to state that the tenure of the judges should be a life one or only until a certain age. They did not make such an enactment then, but we have the right to do it now. That is why we are introducing this legislation. The provision does not go as far as my hon. friend from Muskoka would wish it to go, but I am afraid we have no jurisdiction to extend it to other courts than the federal courts, namely the Supreme Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court of Canada.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
While the minister is upon
that point may I ask if there is any special provision in the British North America Act with respect to the retirement of county court judges? There was an amendment put through, if I remember correctly, in the year 1913 or the year 1914, providing for the compulsory retirement of county court judges [DOT] upon reaching the age of seventy-five years. Is there any special provision in the British North America Act which provides for legislation of that character?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
No.
Mr. BOY'S: Is it suggested that such legislation was ultra vires?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: No, not at all, but 1 would point out that section 99 applies only to the judges of the superior courts.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: And the Exchequer court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: No, the superior courts. We have no right to deal with judges of the superior courts to the extent of restricting their tenure of office, but there is no such provision applicable to the county court judges, who have not been considered as members of the superior or high courts.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: What I thought was that their commission appointed them for life subject to good conduct but subject to removal as a result of impeachment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
There is nothing in the British North America Act preventing us from dealing with the tenure of office of the county court judges, but section 99 prevents

Judges Act Amendment
us from dealing with the tenure of office of superior court or high court judges. That is where the distinction comes in.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I have great respect for the views of the minister but I do not think that was the opinion of the Minister of Justice at the time I refer to. I remember this very matter coming before the House more than ten years ago, and I discussed that feature with the then minister, pointing out that if it was necessary to retire county court judges at seventy-five it was probably quite as necessary to retire judges of the Supreme court at the same age, because they would be just as likely to suffer from ill-health, infirmity or otherwise, as county court judges did and as they were required to deal with matters of far greater concern and importance than county court judges the necessity for compulsory retirement might be even greater.
I recall that his answer to me at that time was that the matter was under consideration, and he hoped to deal with it. He did not say there was no jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: Still the records of the department show that was the obstacle in the way of carrying the idea out with regard to the judges of the high courts or the superior courts. I was reading in the library that in the country to the south they have the same conditions with regard to their federal courts. The constitution of the United States enacts that the judges of these courts shall be appointed and remain in office during good behaviour, and the government has never been able, although it has tried in many instances, to make their retirement compulsory. The United States has endeavoured to deal with the situation by giving a pension equal to their full salary to judges who, having been in office at least ten years and reaching the age of seventy, desire to be superannuated. That was an invitation to them to retire, because they would have a pension equal to their salary; but experience shows that most of them preferred to remain on the bench, even though they were given the right to a full pension when they reached the age of seventy. Fortunately we. have not the same obstacle to meet as far as our federal courts are concerned, and I have come to the conclusion, having not only consulted with but received suggestions from the members of the bar and I might even say from members of the judiciary themselves, that this is a good provision to enact. That is why I am introducing these bills.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: I desire to put myself on record as being opposed to all life appointments. I think they are bad-bad in substance and in fact. I might make the suggestion to the Minister of Justice that if the government is so anxious to reform the Senate it might put into effect an age limit just as in the case of the judges, and that would be something that would work to the benefit of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: I would feel like agreeing with my 'hon. friend in that regard.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
Coming back to the subject under consideration I would say that the principle involved in life appointments is a bad one. There is no question about it in my mind. We could take any man in this House, place him in a position where he is responsible to no one, give him wide power, as we do, leave him there for twenty or twenty-five years, and then we should find in many cases that he was unfit to carry out the responsibility we had entrusted to him. In all kinds of life-animal, vegetable and human- there is a period of growth, development and decay. We cannot get away from that fact; and distasteful as the idea is to us, there comes a point in every man's life where he no longer has the maximum of efficiency. That is true not only physically but mentally. The Great war proved, for example, that people subjected to tremendous physical and mental strain were less efficient after the age of twenty-eight than before. They cannot come back, so to speak. That is true in all walks of life. It is true in the physical sphere. I have under my hand the ages of the men on the bench and they run 87, 75, and so on, for some six or eight of them. I say without hesitation, speaking as a medical man, that the time of maximum efficiency in their life had passed long ago. I know there are some exceptional men who are apparently brilliant at am advanced age, but if they are put to the test I say emphatically that they cannot carry out a sustained effort as they could some years ago.
All you have to do is to carry the knowledge a little further, to go into other spheres of life. For example, in this country there is hardly a university to-day that does not make it compulsory for its professors to retire at from sixty-five to seventy years of age. We have the same regulations in our civil service. In our railways men are retired at sixty-four or sixty-five years of age. We have the same thing in the army and in the navy. We have it also in business life for different reasons and causes. The people retire them and put younger men in their places.	When the late Sir William Van
Horne, I think it was, retired from the presi-
10S2

Judges Act Amendment
deney of the Canadian Pacific railway, I quite remember reading his statement that he was retiring in order to make way for a younger man, the late Lord S'haughnessy. The latter in turn retired and we have Mr. Beatty who, I believe, is only forty-eight years of age and who has been for a number of years directing that large corporation. I have in my hand a list that I copied from the Toronto Globe giving the ages of men at the heads of the large institutions of this country. Sir Henry Thornton is only fifty-eight. I think the Prime Minister of this country is only fifty-two or fifty-three, and the oldest minister in the cabinet is fifty-eight.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: No-sixtyeight.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
At any rate, the principle is that this is a young man's country; this is a young man's age, and when we stick to antiquated methods of leaving people in responsible positions, where they have great power such as they have on the bench, until they are eighty or ninety years of age, we are not doing justice to the country. Other countries are getting rid of this sort of thing. In Great Britain they are retiring county judges at the age of sixty-five. In the United States I believe judges are elected only for short terms. I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to this clipping-I do not know whether or not it is correct-from the Baltimore Sun of January 3t. Speaking about the age limit for judges in the United States it say-s:
Former Justice Charles E. Hughes, discussing the proposed seventy-year age limit for members of the Supreme Court of the United States

So they must have a bill there to retire them.
-agrees that a limit is proper, but he would raise it to seventy-five years for this court. Of course, any limit must be an arbitrary one, retiring at times judges competent to carry on their work; but there have been instances in this tribunal of the grave danger of permitting it to go on without any limit at all on the age of its members. Occasions have arisen not infrequently when justices who, everybody knew, were not in mental or physical condition properly to perform their duties were sitting in this court and, presumably, helping to frame opinions on questions of the greatest and most far-reaching importance.
This is something that is interesting the people not only of this country but of Great Britain and the United States. I would like to ask the Minister of Justice this question: Is there anything more absurd than to leave it to a man who is advanced in years to sit 
in judgment on himself as to whether or not he is fit to carry on? It seems to>
me that such a proposition is ridiculous. In the case of our judges we apply no age limit. We say to them that they may retire, buf we allow them to decide whether they are fit or unfit to carry on. I recognize the difficulties which the Minister of Justice pointed out. I read the British North America Act and I thought section 99 would probably make this resolution unworkable. The proposition I want to make to the minister is this-

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order. In the orders of the day there is this notice of motion standing in the name of the hon. member:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable in the interests of the Dominion of Canada that all judges be retired on reaching seventy-five years of age.
I think the hon. member 'is discussing his motion rather than that of the Minister of Justice. Is that right?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I think my remarks
have been quite in accord with the principle of the resolution. The Minister of Justice admitted that. The only difference between the Minister of Justice and myself is this: I quite agree as regards everything he is doing only he is not going far enough to suit me. I also realize the difficulties in his way. As a layman I read the British North America Act and I thought I was up against section 99. But what I ask him to do in the interest of Canada is this: He told us last night that an inter-provincial conference was going to be held. A subject like this is not very controversial; certainly it does not override any provincial rights. Cannot this be taken up on that occasion so that we may get the consent of the provinces in order that next year the minister can bring in a bill to make this legislation workable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I would certainly be
pleased to submit the suggestion of my hon. friend to such a conference.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
At a later date, when we
come to the estimates, I hope to have something to say on pensions for judges and others. In view of that I would like to ask the minister for his justification of what I admit has always been the practice, namely, of giving large pensions to those who have been receiving large salaries, not to all, but picking out certain classes to which judges belong. What is the justification for giving two-thirds of the salary as an annuity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
It is the law at the
present time, not only in Canada but in other

Judges Act Amendment
countries. Prior to three years ago, apart from the section which gives a pension of two-thirds of their salary to judges who had been fifteen years in office or who were afflicted with some disability, we had another provision which gave them the right to their full salary as a pension after a certain number of years of service and after they reached a certain age. This provision we repealed three years ago and no such pension is now being paid to the judges of Canada, although such a provision, as I stated in my main remarks, still applies in the United States. I think we are far from being more generous to our judges than other countries are. I might show to my hon. friend the resolutions I have received from bar associations and various other bodies in Canada complaining bitterly that the judges are not receiving a sufficient salary or a sufficient pension, and that the best men at the bar decline a judgeship on that account; but I do not think that we will ask for an increase this session. However, I really believe that the present scale of pension, especially when you compare it with what is paid in other countries, is justified.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I am afraid the- minister
has not answered my question. The minister would not justify it because it has been done here, or because it has been done in other countries. The salary the judges receive is probably less than an efficient lawyer can make, but at the same time the salary is still sufficient to enable the judge himself to provide for his old age. There must be other ground that the minister must take if he wishes to justify this. Would he not go a little deeper and attempt to justify it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I must admit I would
have to change the law and reduce the pensions, and my friend has not convinced me that I should do that.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: I expected to see the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George rise to protest in righteous indignation against this resolution, just as he and the member for Toronto did the other night on the old age pension bill. Then he spoke of the wrongfulness of paternalism; of the desirability that people in Canada should be taught the very good lesson of thrift, to save out of their very meagre earnings sufficient to provide for their own old age; that they should not come upon this country as paupers and ask parliament to provide for them after they had passed the age limit for work. But I did not notice the hon. gentleman rise and apply the same principle in this case that he applied in the case of the old age pensions.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: May I ask which member for Toronto the hon. gentleman refers to?

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
He sits here. I do not
know his constituency, but it is Mr. Hocken.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext: He does not sit there.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
That' is the gentleman,
at any rate-Mr. Hocken. Both those hon. gentlemen rose and emphasized that citizens of Canada who were getting the enormous sum of fifty or sixty or seventy cents an hour should be taught the lesson of thrift, should save something out of their meagre earnings in order to provide for their own old age, and not become indigents and paupers upon the country. Here we have gentlemen getting $12,000 a year, and nobody rises to say that they should be thrifty and provide for their own old age. Nobody says that they should not be granted a pension. In the other case there was considerable difficulty in getting a provision for a pension of even ten dollars a month, and then after the old age pensioner died the authorities took power to take over his house to reooup themselves. - I do not see anything in this resolution empowering the government to take over the judge's house in order to recoup the country for the pension he receives in his lifetime. I am not exactly objecting to this resolution, but I do point out that the citizens of Canada who wield the hammer and the spade should receive a pension, and a comfortable pension just as much as these others, for their work is just as honourable and just as needful to the country as that of the judges who sit upon the Supreme court bench.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
Will the proposed bill in any
way affect the quorum of the Supreme court or the quorum by consent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
No, it is not intended
to affect that section of the act.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL JUDGE, SUPREME COURT-RETIREMENTS, SUPREME AND EXCHEQUER COURTS
speechtext:
I do not want to offer any
observation which is going to interfere in any way with the efficient administration of justice in Canada. I realize the importance of the Supreme court, but I do not feel that the minister has made out a case for increasing the number of the members of the court. He has said very little to warrant an increase *which is going to impose upon the country an additional burden of $12,000 a year. In my own province, and I presume it is the same in others, we have appellate courts. There are no extra judges for these courts, unless they are taken from the judges assigned to the trial courts, and if that is done, it has to be at the expense of efficiency in the trial court. At the present time, with
Judges Act Amendment

a quorum in the Supreme court of five-and I certainly think the judges should sit in an odd number, instead of an even, because it is desirable to have a majority decision-if the quorum is not being altered, I do not think the addition of one judge should be required. I do not know who it is that has asked for this legislation, whether it is the judges of the Supreme court 'themselves, because of the amount of work they have to do, 'but it would seem to me to be in order for the committee to be enlightened as to the number of cases that come before the court, to indicate whether the judges of that court have more work than can toe conveniently attended to and have not sufficient time to properly study, consider and dispose of the cases that come before them. It should be demonstrated that they cannot under present conditions do their work satisfactorily. I happen to know that in my own province there is a tremendous congestion of business at times, and I believe there is even greater necessity there for an increase in number. I am inclined to ithe view that there is greater necessity for an increase in the number of judges who now have to take care of the work of the Supreme court of Ontario, and probably the other provinces, than there is in the number of judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. With a court composed of six, with a quorum of five, and a consent quorum of four-and the work has always been done well in the -past-you will always have one extra judge, and perhaps two extra judges, to do the work of -the court. I think the minister should show the committee some very substantial reason for putting the country to the -expense of another $12,000 a year for all time to coim-e, and that w-e should be given some information as to the number of cases the judges have to deal with, and other facts to indicate that they are not able to discharge their duties efficiently without 'being overworked, before we are called upon to vote this money.

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
1.	That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide or arrange through a company to be formed under the Companies Act, for a mail, passenger and freight sendee, in accordance with the West Indies Trade agreement, 1926.
2.	That the securities to be issued by the company may be guaranteed by the Dominion as to principal and interest to an amount not exceeding, without the authority of parliament an aggregate of $10,000,000.
3.	That the proceeds of sale or disposition of the securities shall be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance; and the entire stock ownership of the company shall be issued to His Majesty in the right of the Dominion in consideration of the guarantee.
4.	That any of the boats now operated by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, may be transferred to the company on a reasonable valuation and on terms to be approved by the governor in council, and if transferred to be operated by individual companies, such companies shall issue to the company all their capital stock to indemnify the crown against liability in respect of the guarantee.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Marcil in the chair.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION OP COMPANY TO PROVIDE STEAMSHIP SERVICE
speechtext:
This is a very important
resolution, and one to which I personally must take strong objection. I will briefly outline my reasons for so doing, although when the minister brings down the bill it may contain safeguarding features which will in some measure meet my objections. With regard to the first paragraph, which states that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for mail and passenger service and so on to the West Indies, to that I can have no objection; we certainly should implement our undertakings and arrange to take care of that traffic. But to the suggestion that it be done through a company to be formed under the Companies Act, and to the next paragraph which provides for a guarantee to such company in principal and interest to an extent of $10,000,000, I object. Naturally I am not in possession of all the facts, but I recall an announcement appearing in the press a few days ago to the effect that a couple of gentlemen, Mr. Raymond and Mr. McDougall, had organized a company to take over Vickers
10S6

West Indies Trade Agreement
Limited in the city of Montreal for the purpose of building these vessels. Vickers Limited is an old, well-established firm; I presume that in recent years they must have had some difficulty in making a return on capital invested, since shipbuilding has certainly not been a very prosperous business in Canada, but these well known gentlemen could not be properly classified, I think, as eminent shipbuilders. However, they have formed a company for the purpose of building these ships and now we find the government coming forward with a proposal in which they guarantee the principal and' interest to the extent of 110,000,000. I rather think I overhear the minister say it has nothing to do with this bill, but there is a rather touching synchronization, to put it mildly.
Whether or not that group is behind this venture, the fact remains that it is proposed to guarantee $10,000,000 of principal and interest of a company which shall do certain things. Then if you follow the resolution a step further you will find that it is also giving power to turn over some of the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, on a valuation and terms to be approved by the Governor in Council; that is section 4. It is also stated) that the capital stock is to be turned over to the crown as an indemnity against liability in respect of the guarantee. We have the Canadian Government Merchant Marine owming the ships and the government owning the company; now we propose to pass legislation which will turn those ships now owned by the government over to another company whose stock shall be guaranteed by the government. Thus, unless the resolution be explained in some manner certainly contrary to its present wording, an amazing situation is disclosed. How we can justify to the people of Canada the creation of a new company or companies and the guaranteeing of new stock and new capital for the purpose of taking over property which we already own is beyond me. I know there are those who criticize the present Canadian Government Merchant Marine and say that it was not a good venture and so forth, but the fact of the matter is -that we have suffered all the loss a country can possibly suffer through a venture of this kind. That is history now; that is behind us. An opportunity presents itself to make the Canadian 'Government Merchant Marine pay by simply utilizing the machinery we now have; we can construct new ships if necessary or we can use the present ships to give this service without creating any new company and without guaranteeing capital for any private group. So without having the details of the bill be-

fore me I say I am absolutely opposed to this proposal and particularly to section 2 of the resolution. I hope the committee will become thoroughly seized of the significance of that section, which reads:
That the securities to be issued by the company may be guaranteed by the Dominion as to principal and interest to an amount not exceeding, without the authority of parliament, an aggregate of $10,000,000.
The plain and simple reading of that section is that the government is asking for the right to guarantee for principal and interest the capital of a new company to the extent of $10,000,000, and it is intimated in the words "without the authority of parliament" that they expect the company to come back later and ask for a further guarantee. That is, if the $10,000,000 is not sufficient the company may ask for a further amount to 'be guaranteed. In other words, certain gentlemen unnamed in the resolution, without the investment of one dollar, are to get $10,000,000 of Dominion government money, because a bond guaranteed by the government is just the same as money; any security guaranteed by this government is equal to the government's own security. We are dipping into the treasury of Canada and giving this companv, whose personnel is unnamed in the resolution, $10,000,000 of the money of Canada to organize a new company to render a service which we already have an organization capable of performing. It is a most astounding proposal, and speaking for myself it is my intention as we proceed to scrutinize every step as closely as possible. At this time, however, I wish to register my opposition to the proposal as disclosed in the resolution.

speechtext:
Perhaps my friend would permit me to make an explanation to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), which would clear matters up. I am pleased that my hon. friend said that if the resolution meant what he thought it meant he would' oppose it; I can assure him that when he examines the bill based on the resolution, a great deal of what he describes as astounding will vanish. As to guaranteeing the bonds of gentlemen unnamed and thereby making them 'a present of $10,000,000 of the credit of this country, there is absolutely no such intention. The guarantee will be given and the shares will be held by the Minister of Finance in the same manner as the shares of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the shares of the Canadian National Railway Company are held. The $10,000,000 guarantee given to this institution will be in fact given to the

West Indies Trade Agreement
Canadian National Railway System. The manner of dealing with it is rendered necessary by the nature of the business itself. My hon. friend is, I am sure, not aware of the fact that each one of the ships now operated by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is operated by a separate company. A system such as this, I am given to understand, has proved to be the most satisfatcory way of operating steamships, so that criticism of the proposal from the point of view of extending the guarantee of the government of Canada to private interests entirely falls to the ground. There is no private interest involved in this proposal in any way, shape or form. A new corporation is being established1-indeed it may >be a number of new corporations, one for each ship-in order to deal specifically with the West Indies service, which is a new service demanding special types of ships and one which we desire to keep absolutely separate in operation and accounting from the ordinary Canadian Government Merchant Marine. It is desirable in view of the West Indies trade agreement that the shipping feature of it should be a thing apart from the general operation of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, especially as one of the stipulations of the treaty itself is that the colonies concerned, the various West Indian colonies, should themselves contribute a subsidy for the maintenance of this particular steamship line. Hence it is desirable to incorporate it separately from the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I think that deals with the main objection advanced by my hon, friend.
As is well known, the government of Canada has for many years been paying a subsidy for the operation of a steamship service to the West Indies. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will be here-he has just come in now-and he will deal with the trade treaty and the subsidy features of this matter. Suffice it for me to say that the government has on two occasions, if not three, advertised for subsidy tenders from existing steamship lines for operation of the service called for by the West Indies trade agreement. The results of our call for tenders will be dealt with in detail by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I feel sure that when those facts are before it the House will agree that the best way of dealing with this West Indies situation is through the medium of our own Canadian National organization, and the financing of a government owned steamship service to the West Indies under the provisions of the trade agreement.
What is proposed is to form a separate company for operating purposes, for the
reasons I have just outlined. In order to live up to the agreement it is necessary for us to put into operation to the eastern group of inlands a fortnightly service, passenger, mail and freight, from Canadian ocean ports all the year round, calling each way at Bermuda, St. Kitts, Nevis, Antigua, Montserrat, Dominica St. Lucia, Barbados, St. Vincent, Grenada, Tobago, Trinidad and Demerara; and also a fortnightly freight service from Canadian river ports in summer and Canadian ocean ports in winter, calling at St. Kitts, Antigua, Barbados, Trinidad and Demerara. That is for the eastern group.
For the western group our treaty obligations call for a fortnightly passenger, mail and freight service between St. Lawrence ports in summer and such Canadian ocean ports in winter as may be designated by the Canadian government, calling both ways at Bermuda, the Bahamas, and Kingston, Jamaica; and also a fortnightly freight service between the said Canadian ports and Kingston, Jamaica, direct, alternating with the previous service; also a fortnightly passenger and freight service between Kingston, Jamaica, and British Honduras, to be operated by a small steamer connecting at Kingston with the passenger vessels. It is proposed to give these services to the eastern groups by operating three passenger, mail and freight motor ships of 5,800 tons deadweight, 14 knots speed, with accommodation for 1001 first class passengers, 30 second class passengers, 100 steerage or deck passengers, and cold storage facilities. Freight services for the eastern group will be operated by four freight vessels of 4,300 tons deadweight, speed about 10 knots, and at present the property of the crown.
I may here dispose of another point that was troubling my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. Any vessels which are disposed of by the merchant marine to this new company for the operation of the West Indies service may be paid for out of the proceeds of guaranteed bonds, and the amount so paid may be paid to the Minister of Finance and will constitute a reduction to that extent of the present liability of the merchant marine. Or the notes held by the Minister of Finance may be simply transferred to apply to the new company.

But as to the cost of operating these boats-having made some calculations myself and being familiar with the operations of steamships, and bearing in mind the calculations of others who have been operating steamships-I say that the annual deficit on the operations of this West Indian service and treaty will be at least two millions a year. I stand by that statement. I am satisfied that is the figure which will materialize, and I say that this contract, in connection with the treaty which has been entered into, will be very disastrous to this Dominion.

There has been so
much cross questioning that I hardly know where to start my remarks and supplement what has already been said by the Minister of Railways. At the present time we are paying $340,000 a year for a service to the West Indian islands which is not satisfactory either as to frequency or as to capacity. At the time of the conference of 1925, a better service was arranged along the lines of the service which had been provided at the conference of 1920, but which had not been carried out. When
the tenders were called for as mentioned by my colleague the Minister of Railways, no satisfactory tender was received-in fact no tender was received for the western service via the western islands and Jamaica. The government was not able to award a tender, nor was it satisfied at that time that it had exhausted the field of those who might wish to figure. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat spoke to me at the first part of this session before Christmas, and we again opened the tenders in order to let the com-panj' in which he is interested or others tender again, but without success. I have very carefully prepared estimates by the officers of the Canadian National railways who have submitted to us a set of figures which, if correct will1 save this country much more money than if we continue to pay subsidies.
I have taken the trouble to compile some figures as to what it costs to continue a steamship subsidy and I think it is worth while for the committee to know this. I think the senior member for Halifax will be glad to have this information. It is true the government is asking for a $10,000,000 capital outlay to provide a frequent service as called for by the treaty, and it is stated that the interest on a capital outlay of $10,000,000 is not a small amount. But if we continue to pay money in the form of subsidies for which we get absolutely nothing back and on which we lose the interest for all time to come, the amount involved runs into a considerable sum. Since 1889 and 1890 we have been paying subsidies for the West Indies service. The amount started at $49,942. It reached $73,000 in 1901. It continued to grow until in 1905 it reached $134,000. In 1910 and 1911 the subsidy amounted to $144000. I will not weary the committee with the figures, but finally in 1925-26 it reached $318,000. The Dominion of Canada on this West Indies service has now paid out in cash $6,593,000. That, computed at 5 per cent interest annually since we have gone into this business, means that this country has now contributed to the British West Indies service $13,930,000.

speechtext: To what firm in particular were the subsidies granted?

speechtext:
I have not the names
to give to the hon. member. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company have been the successful tenderers on the last few occasions. The point I wish to deal with is this, that while we have been paying out S340.0GO for a service which is not satisfactory to the West Indian islands, our own officers now estimate that under the plan submitted by the Minister of Railways we are going to have an operating

West Indies Trade Agreement
deficit of $764,000. That is much more money than we have been paying out in subsidies but it is not to be compared to what private firms would have asked for the same service. The senior member for Halifax is unquestionably a good shipping man; he knows what it costs to run this service and make money out of it. No man in this House is in a better position than he is to judge; but I am inclined to think that he is underestimating the possibilities of trade on the western route. His firm did not see fit to figure on that route. They did give us a figure on the eastern service for which they are now obtaining $340,000, but the figure which they gave us was $582,000 for that service, which is one-half of the service. The western service they refused altogether to figure on.
As to the prophecy of the hon. gentleman, I must admit that I am not sufficiently acquainted with the trade in the West Indies or sufficient of a prophet to estimate what may develop or to contradict the hon. gentleman, *but I have sufficient faith in the officers who have compiled the estimate to make this prophecy, that the hon. gentleman's estimate of a deficit of $2,000,000 will be shown to be absurd in the first two years of operation and more absurd at the end of the five years. Those acquainted with this trade have a feeling that much business will develop.
The subject is such an old one that I do not think it is necessary for me to review the history of this service since back in 1890 when Sir George Foster made his first attempt to effect trade treaties with the West Indies. I think hon. members do not want to be wearied with a review of the whole series of events leading up to the 1920 conference.

Under this plan the estimated deficit the first year is $818,000. If the boats were all built in Great Britain the estimated deficit would be $675,000. The plan which the minister submits is an average plan with three of the boats built in Canada

and two built in Great Britain with an estimated deficit of $764,000. I am inclined to think-and I believe hon. members will agree with me-that we are not prone to overestimate deficits. It is not very long since 1921 when we came into this House and we were told that the deficits on the National railways could not be improved and that the system should be sold.

speechtext:
I said some on this
side. It was even said by one hon. gentleman that the system should be sold for a dollar. There is not a man now who would sell the National railways for a dollar; there is not a man who is not proud of the success of the National railways. This steamship system is going to give to the Shippers, to the passenger trade of this country, to our sister dominions and colonies an opportunity to do more trade and more travelling within the British Empire. It is going to provide a passenger service which I believe the people of this country will appreciate.
The trade of the West Indies and the trade of Canada do not in any way conflict. It is needless to read a long list of commodites which are exchanged between these two parts of the British Empire, but they do not conflict in any way. We have further plans for the development of trade with the West Indies, which plans we will reveal to the House at a later date. They will not involve an expenditure of such magnitude as this. After going over the trade figures with the West Indian islands on commodities which do not conflict with our products, I am firmly convinced that the trade figures, when this service is instituted, will reveal a very marked increase inasmuch as we shall be buying through Canadian ports many commodities which now come to us through United States channels. When I was speaking on the budget I made the remark that it is difficult to rely on statistics. We do more business with the West Indies and Cuba than we are credited with because a good deal of dt passes through United States channels. There will not be as great an increase of business between Canada and the West Indies by virtue of this service as some people might imagine; but there will be more direct business through Canadian ports and over a Canadian system, and that

West Indies Trade Agreement
is the very thing that is going to make that service pay better than most people believe at the present time. If our freight can be brought direct from the West Indies, as we propose it shall be in these boats having the necessary cold storage capacity, we shall be diverting a certain amount of trade that now comes through the United States and is credited under Canadian imports as being of American origin, whereas in reality it is of West Indian origin. While I make that point,
I want to be correctly interpreted. I doubt if the service is going to increase to such a great extent our business with the West Indies. It will to some extent, but there is only a certain volume of business that can be done there, and the increase is not going to be so much an increase in the volume of trade as in diversion of trade from American channels to Canadian channels and Canadian ports. To me, Mr. Chairman, that is the most important part of this service. According to our [DOT]latest figures for 1926, in bananas, grape fruit, cocoanuts, spices, and so forth, we are buying from the West Indies somewhere about $15,000,000 worth of merchandise a year, but I firmly believe that actually we are buying over $20,000,000 worth of West Indian products. I believe that fifty per cent of our goods from the West Indies comes through American channels. We are selling to the West Indies about $17,200,000 worth of goods, but 1 believe that into the same territory goes a very considerable amount of Canadian export through American channels by reason of the scarcity of Canadian tonnage.
This service, Mr. Chairman, is designed to do two things. It is designed to give river trade in the summer to Montreal, and to divide the trade between Halifax and St. John in the winter, serving equally both transportation companies, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. We as a government feel that we have to keep faith with the agreements of 1920 and 1925. We feel this is part of our contribution to empire unity. We realize that the cost is not going to .be small, but we feel that we would be very much less than honest if we did not put on this service, and I say frankly to the House. Mr. Chairman, that I do not believe, after two calls for tenders, that the service can be put on in any other way than we are offering to the House to-night. We searched the field and endeavoured in every way possible to give every private interest the opportunity to figure on this service. We considered a subsidy also before we finally arrived
at the conclusion we arrived at, and which we are now submitting to the House. If the service is installed, I am as hopeful as I was in 1921 of the National railway. I believe the figures as estimated will be found to be practically correct. We have discouraged any super-optimism on the part of the Canadian National Steamship Company officials as to what their probable earnings would be. We have figured from a very careful basis so far as the government is concerned, and my colleague the Minister of Finance has been most insistent that no undue optimism should be used which would result in him being asked to come back and apologize for the estimate in five years. That is all as a government we could do in compiling the figures.
I sincerely hope that the estimate of the senior member for Halifax is quite wrong.
I personally think it is. I believe that with the growth and development of the service, the estimates as compiled by the officials will be found to be very nearly correct.
Just one word more with regard to the question of building these boats in Canada or in Great Britain. It is not a very serious matter whether all these boats * are built in Canada, or whether three of them are built in Canada and two in Great Britain. It is a matter of $100,000 annually. It is a matter of policy for this House to determine whether they are prepared to face about another $100,000 annual deficit on the plan we have prepared in order to have all the ships built in Canada, or whether they are willing to effect another $100,000 saving annually by having them all built in Great Britain. We have chosen the middle course. We have been informed by the officials, in making their estimates as to the advisability of building two ships in Great Britain, that two of them can best be built in British shipyards on account of the refrigeration system that is required. My hon. friend a moment ago said that the refrigeration system was installed after the boat was built. Quite true, but it is on the installation of the refrigeration system that the British builders' figures are so very much lower than the Canadian builders' figures. It may be quite possible to import from Great Britain refrigeration plants and install them here, but the National railway experts felt that the two boats with the heavy refrigeration could best be built in Britain, and that the other three boats could best be built in Canada. Speaking for myself-I am not speaking for the Minister of Railways-

West Indies Trade Agreement
I do not believe the committee in charge of this matter would have any objection, if -the House is in favour, and when the details are asked, to having all these boats built in Canada if it can be shown that they can be built economically in this country. I have no brief for either plan. We submit this as a middle course on the recommendation of those estimating on the service, so that we may have some figure to come to parliament with. When the plans are ready, they will be submitted to British and Canadian yards, and we believe that about $10,000,000 will provide the service asked for. Further than that, Mr. Chairman, there is very little I can contribute to the debate.

Not only that, but if the capitalization of the ships is increased by reason of the fact that they are constructed in Canada, then we are saddling an extra capitalization on that trade between the maritime provinces and the West Indies. No Canadian can ignore that, but it seems to me that the difficulty can be got over in another way, without adopting the middle course, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests. I do not think there is any justification for the middle course. I think the government should decide on a definite policy, whether they are prepared to pay the extra price and have these ships constructed in Canada, or whether they should permit the officers of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine to procure these ships in the markets of the world at the lowest possible prices. Inasmuch as practically the whole of the settlement will have to be by compromise arrangements with the provincial governments, or particularly with the municipalities through the provincial governments, it is largely a matter of the allocation of the amounts, because the properties will never realize the full amounts of the liens and obligations against them. Therefore there will have to be an allocation of the amounts, and I would like to cite one instance. At the moment there is an arrangement which we are endeavouring to put into execution whereby we will take all the area around the Bow river, bounded on the south by Medicine Hat and on the north by the Red Deer river and going ten ranges westward; we are endeavouring to put that territory under range conditions once more, and our officers are allocating certain areas with water privileges which we hope to lease rather than sell to ranchers over a long term of years. In most cases it is true that the provincial governments have proceeded under the tax enforcement act and are now the owners of a very large proportion of this property, subject of course to our liens which have priority. We hope to get those lands

Seed Grain and Other Relief
down to a valuation on which reasonable rentals can be secured, to see whether we cannot transform that whole area back to the range conditions which prevailed before homesteading and settlement duties were permitted. So each individual case will have to be dealt with separately, and by that I mean every individual unit. We have a joint board which is advising both governments, and which will make an allocation of the amounts to be received by the crown and by the province for the taxation indebtedness; if there is any further creditor such as a mortgage company, a machinery company or a merchant having claims, the board will settle what proportion each creditor will lose in order to get an adjustment of that claim. That will wipe it off and1 get the land clear of any encumbrance once more.
That, I may say to the committee, is briefly one method of adjusting these claims. The other, of course, is where we are not endeavouring to do that, where there are scattered parcels of land which may be located anywhere in either of these provinces, in which the provincial government is interested with the municipality again behind the provincial government. In those cases representative officers of the two governments will try to arrive at an allocation of the loss to be sustained by each party. That is all the authority we are asking.

speechtext:
I should like to point
out a few facts as to the necessity for this legislation. The municipalities, the loan companies and individuals are all interested. As has been said, these liens date from 1876. About 1910, 1911 and 1912, a great number of people went in and filed on homesteads, and took up preemptions on that land which was then thrown open for homestead purposes. During the years that followed many farmers found it necessary to give up, and in one year, namely in 1915, security was taken to the extent of $12,000,000 for the relief that was given out. There were good crops in 1915 and 1916, and a great part of these obligations have been paid off. Owing to the lean years which followed, however, many people have found themselves quite unable to pay their obligations. When the settlers went in homes were built and stock purchased; school districts were organized and small towns were built up. But as the result of a succession of dry years these small villages were almost deserted, and the school districts could not carry on. I know of one municipality where thirteen school districts were in operation but where now there is only one. In the Tilley area which the minister has mentioned there were formerly fifty-seven school districts in operation; now there are only thirteen. As the people moved out they left their debts behind1, and of course the merchants, machinery companies, and others have suffered to a greater or less extent. Those people could do nothing else. It was impossible for them to pay their debts, and through no fault of their own they found themselves in that condition. Many of them have left, and the Tilley commission found that in one district in which they made investigation 85 per cent of the farms were deserted. In any case there is not sufficient security left to satisfy these relief claims. At the present time I understand there is no one who has authority to cancel those claims, so I think this legislation will help to improve matters to some extent. Those claims for relief were placed against the land prior to the municipal or school claim for taxes, and prior to any claim that the mortgage companies may have had and those having claims were not notified. Where mortgage companies have instituted foreclosure proceedings and taken over the land they find that these prior

1106	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-New Brunswick
claims have rendered their equity null. One large insurance company has discontinued the payment of taxes on their extensive holdings, and this makes it very difficult for the farmers who have remained to pay the taxes for local purposes. In many cases the municipalities have taken over this land for the non-payment of taxes, but they found prior liens registered against the land, and in many cases the liens are of greater value than the land itself. For instance I know of one quarter for which the municipality was offered $500 but against which the amount of liens was more than $1,000.
This legislation is particularly important in the interest of those farmers who are remaining on the land, and who have struggled along through all the bad years in the effort to maintain their homes. If that land was made, available at a low rate for grazing or for purposes such as that, it could be made use of. Eates should be regulated according to the number of acres required to care for so many head of stock. These people would thus be piaced in a much better position to carry on and to maintain their homes, and we should try to keep them there because they are the greatest assets that we have. Their experience is of great value. It is necessary that some organization should have the right to reduce or cancel these claims. In many cases they should be cancelled outright. There is little security left. The men who are there have a debt that is twelve or fifteen years old, and I really believe the department should deal very generously with those claims and see that fairness is done to all parties.

As has been well pointed out by the Minister of Public Works, this money is being appropriated for the construction of a post office building at Baie St. Paul, which is the chief town in the county of Charlevoix. The county of Charlevoix, including Baie St. Paul, is one of the largest districts below Quebec. The building in which the post office is located comprises the court house, the magistrate's court, which holds its sittings there, and the registration office, and to the post office a very small room is allotted by the county council. The accommodation is totally inadequate for the postal service in that district. The post office has been, I might say, sponging on the county council for the last twenty-five or thirty years. The post office has hardly as much space as the ordinary room allotted to members of the House here, and-that is where the sorting and distribution of the mail has to take place for the whole district. Baie St. Paul is a distributing centre for the mails for the village, parish and -the municipality of St. Laurent, as well as for the municipalities and rural routes such as St. Hilarion du Lac, St. Gabriel, Clairvaux de Charlevoix and He aux Coudres, with four post offices to serve.

I might point out to my hon. friend that it is not a new thing to construct post offices in other parts of the province of Quebec and elsewhere where the population is not so large as it is at this place, because the government that preceded the Union government in 1914, just at the outbreak of the war, when it was very necessary to economize, put up a post office building costing over $35,000 at Murray Bay, where the population was about the same size as at Baie St. Paul to-day. I say that if it was necessary for the Borden government of that day, on the outbreak of the war, when economy was very necessary, to spend that large amount of money, we can well afford to give to the district of Baie St. Paul to-day the same postal facilities that other parts of the province of Quebec and the country at large have been enjoying for years past. In view of these conditions I feel that the committee should not be reluctant to grant this vote.
